title: He wants an MRI for ten days of back pain
objective: Classify low back pain by duration (acute under 6 weeks, chronic beyond 12 weeks) and explain why routine imaging is held back: disc degeneration shows up in more than 80% of adults over 50, with or without symptoms
secondaryObjectives: Treat new urinary retention, bowel dysfunction, saddle anesthesia or new bilateral leg weakness as possible cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency needing immediate referral

Screen low back pain for red flags: prior cancer or unexplained weight loss; infection risk such as recent spinal procedures, intravenous drug use, immunosuppression or fever; fracture risk such as trauma, long-term corticosteroids, osteoporosis or age over 70

brief.situation: 08:30 in an outpatient orthopedic clinic (direct access). You are the physical therapist. Mr. Okoye, 46, a warehouse supervisor, has had low back pain for 10 days since lifting a pallet, with pain down his left leg. He wants 'an MRI to see what's wrong' before he does any exercise.
handover: Intake form: no prior back surgery; takes ibuprofen; no other medicines.

Clinic policy follows the national suspected cauda equina pathway: suspected cauda equina syndrome goes to the hospital emergency department with emergency MRI the same hour; tell his primary care physician.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Each question or test takes the time on its button. Decide what to ask, what it means and what to do.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Does Mr. Okoye need an MRI? Classify his back pain, say why imaging is usually held back, and what is different today.

parts.label: Classification and imaging
parts.criteria: Acute low back pain (10 days, under 6 weeks) with radicular pain; routine imaging is held back in acute back pain because disc degeneration is found in most adults (over 80% over 50) with or without symptoms, so a scan without red flags does not change care.
parts.modelAnswer: This is acute low back pain, 10 days, with left leg pain. Without red flags I would not image: scans show disc degeneration in most adults, over 80% of those over 50, whether or not they hurt, so a routine MRI would not change what we do.

parts.label: What is different
parts.criteria: New difficulty starting urination, altered saddle sensation and a deficit in both legs: possible cauda equina syndrome, an emergency; no manipulation; hospital with emergency MRI now; tells the primary care physician.
parts.modelAnswer: But he has new difficulty starting to urinate, altered saddle sensation and signs in both legs. That is possible cauda equina syndrome. No manipulation; he goes to the emergency department now for an emergency MRI, and I tell his physician.

expertPath.text: History: 10 days, acute low back pain with left leg pain. Screen the red flags: none for cancer, infection or fracture.
Ask about bladder, bowel, saddle sensation and sexual function: new hesitancy, altered saddle sensation, tingling in both legs.
Neurologic exam: a deficit in both legs. No manipulation.
Emergency department now for an emergency MRI. Tell his physician.

retention.headline: Retention in the clinic
retention.body: Ask about bladder, bowel and saddle sensation in everyone with back and leg pain, and never manipulate when cauda equina syndrome is possible.

delayed.headline: Sent away without emergency imaging
delayed.body: Holding back routine imaging is right for acute back pain without red flags. Cauda equina symptoms are the exception: hospital with emergency MRI now, not an outpatient scan.

sentNow.headline: Sent for emergency MRI
sentNow.body: You classified his pain as acute, knew why routine imaging is held back, asked the cauda equina questions, avoided manipulation and sent him the same hour. That is the expert path.

sentGaps.headline: Sent, with gaps
sentGaps.body: Check how soon the bladder and saddle questions came, whether anything was done to his spine first, and how long the decision took.

time_up.headline: Still in the clinic
time_up.body: Suspected cauda equina syndrome needs a decision within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Ten days of back pain after lifting is acute low back pain (under 6 weeks). Without red flags, routine imaging is held back because disc degeneration is found in more than 80% of adults over 50 whether or not they hurt, and a scan rarely changes care. But new difficulty starting urination, altered saddle sensation and a deficit in both legs are suspected cauda equina syndrome, which the national pathway sends to a hospital with emergency MRI now. So: no manipulation, emergency department now, and tell his physician.
